i.description: High, front, spread lips — tense and bright, like the ee in “see” but shorter and crisper.

e.description: High-mid, front, spread lips. No real English equivalent — closer to the vowel in “say” but without the glide at the end.

ɛ.description: Lower-mid, front, spread lips. Close to the e in “bed,” a bit more open than [e].

a.description: Low, front, spread lips — the most open vowel in this group, close to the a in “cat.”

y.description: Same tongue position as [i] — high and forward — but with lips tightly rounded, as if starting to whistle.

ø.description: Same tongue position as [e], lips rounded. Say [e], then round your lips without moving your tongue.

œ.description: Same tongue position as [ɛ], lips rounded — a touch more open than [ø].

ɑ.description: Low and further back than [a], lips relaxed rather than rounded. In most of France today this has largely merged with [a] — worth knowing it exists, but don’t worry about distinguishing it by ear yet.

ɔ.description: Low-mid, back, rounded. Close to the o in British “hot.”

o.description: High-mid, back, rounded — closer to the vowel in “go,” but held steady instead of gliding into a w sound.

u.description: High and back, tightly rounded lips — close to “oo” in “food.” Not the same symbol as [y] — [u] is rounded-and-back, [y] is rounded-and-front.

ə.description: Short, central, relaxed — the “uh” sound. Frequently dropped in fast speech: je ne sais pas is often said more like “j’n’sais pas.”

ɑ̃.description: Related to oral [ɑ]. The most open of the four nasal vowels.

ɛ̃.description: Related to oral [ɛ]. Spelled many ways — in, im, ain, ein, yn, ym all land here.

ɔ̃.description: Related to oral [ɔ]. Rounded lips, air through the nose.

œ̃.description: Related to oral [œ]. The rarest of the four — many French speakers today merge it into [ɛ̃], so hearing un and in sound identical is common and not a mistake on their part.

j.description: Identical to English y in “yes.” Also appears spelled -ill- and -il, as in fille and travail.

w.description: Identical to English w in “west.” Usually spelled oi or ou before a vowel.

ɥ.description: The one with no English equivalent: round your lips as if for [y] (the vowel in tu), then glide immediately into the next vowel. Almost always spelled u before another vowel.

p.description: Voiceless, lips together, no puff of air on release — crisper and softer than English p.

b.description: The voiced twin of [p] — lips together, vocal cords buzzing throughout. Essentially identical to English b.

t.description: Voiceless, but dental — tongue touches the back of the upper teeth, not the ridge behind them the way English t does. No puff of air.

d.description: The voiced twin of [t] — same dental tongue position, vocal cords buzzing. Close to English d.

k.description: Voiceless, back of the tongue against the soft palate. Hides behind several spellings: c before a/o/u, qu, and k itself all land here — cave, qui, and kilo all start with [k].

ɡ.description: The voiced twin of [k]. Spelled g before a/o/u, or gu before e/i/y to keep the hard sound — compare gare to guide.

f.description: Voiceless, top teeth on bottom lip — identical to English f. Spelled f or ph.

v.description: The voiced twin of [f] — identical to English v.

s.description: Voiceless, like English s. Spelled s at the start of a word or next to a consonant, ss between vowels, or c/ç before e/i/y.

z.description: The voiced twin of [s]. The spelling trap: a single s between vowels is also [z] — maison is [mɛzɔ̃], not [mɛsɔ̃]. Double it (ss) to get [s] back, as in poisson.

ʃ.description: The “sh” sound, always spelled ch in French — never pronounced like English “ch” in “chip.”

ʒ.description: The voiced twin of [ʃ] — like the s in English “measure.” Spelled j, or g before e/i/y.

m.description: Lips together, air through the nose — identical to English m.

n.description: Tongue tip against the teeth, air through the nose — identical to English n.

ɲ.description: A single consonant — tongue flat against the roof of the mouth — close to the ny in English “canyon,” always spelled gn.

ŋ.description: The “ng” sound in English “sing.” Not native to French, but common in words borrowed from English like parking and camping.

l.description: Lighter and more forward than English l — tongue tip against the teeth the whole time, none of the “dark” back-of-mouth quality English l can have at the end of a word.

ʁ.description: The French R — made in the back of the throat, not with the tip of the tongue the way English R is. The single most distinctive sound in French pronunciation, and the subject of its own full lesson on this site.
